Orchot Tzadikim 24:2: Flattery divides into nine parts. The first: one who recognizes that his fellow is wicked and a deceiver, that he gives a bad name to worthy people, and that he robs his fellow's money — and this person comes and flatters him. And it is not enough that he flatters him and praises him, but he even smooths his tongue and says: "you have done no wrong in what you did" —
Orchot Tzadikim 24:3: in this there are several transgressions and many punishments. The first: he should have rebuked him for his sins. And it is not enough that he does not rebuke him, but he tells him "you have not sinned" and strengthens the hand of evildoers. And this flatterer has a punishment for not having been zealous for the truth. And further: this flatterer places a stumbling-block before the sinner, for when he says "you have not sinned," the sinner will not turn from his evil, and will sin still more — apart from the punishment he incurs for the harm and grief he caused the people the sinner harmed and grieved, and does not repay them or appease them, because of the flattery of this one who justifies the wicked man. And it is said (Proverbs 17:15), "he who justifies the wicked, and he who condemns the righteous, both of them alike are an abomination to the Lord." And if this sinner's transgression is known to the public, and this flatterer flatters him publicly, saying to him, "you are pure and upright" — then he has desecrated the Blessed Name, and this involves religious law and judgment.
Orchot Tzadikim 24:4: And a person is obligated to place himself in danger rather than fall into this iniquity. And our Sages, peace upon them, said of Agrippa, that he was reading from the Torah, and when he reached the verse (Deuteronomy 17:15), "you may not put a foreigner over you," his eyes flowed with tears. They said to him: "you are our brother!" At that moment the enemies of Israel became liable for destruction because they had flattered Agrippa (Sotah 41b).
Orchot Tzadikim 24:5: Also, a judge sitting in judgment should fear no man, as it is said (Deuteronomy 1:17), "you shall not be afraid of the face of any man." And in such flattery there is the punishment for both falsehood and flattery.
Orchot Tzadikim 24:6: The second: one who praises a wicked man before people, whether in his presence or not in his presence. And even though he does not justify him for his bad deeds, but merely says in general terms, "he is a good man" — of this it is said (Proverbs 28:4), "those who forsake the Torah praise the wicked." For this one who praises him, were it not that he had forsaken the Torah, would not have praised one who transgresses it and its words. Also, he should not plead the wicked man's case before people, saying: "is he not doing this good deed? Therefore have compassion on him." And whoever does this is very bad, for the listeners will suppose he is righteous and will give him honor. And there is great danger in honoring the wicked, for when there is honor for the righteous, wise men who are exalted, then all the people will listen to their counsel. And further: others will envy their good deeds, and will increase learning and knowledge will grow, and from [performing a commandment] not for its own sake one comes to [perform it] for its own sake.
Orchot Tzadikim 24:7: And further: there are many people who, upon seeing the splendor of the Torah, will recognize its virtue, and a thought will come into their hearts, and they will study for the sake of the Holy One, blessed be He, with a whole heart. And there is also a good reason in honoring the righteous wise men: for the foundation of a person's soul is to have within it the service, fear, and Torah of the Holy One, blessed be He, and because of this the whole world honors the righteous. It follows that whoever honors the righteous, as it were, upholds and maintains the intent of the Holy One, blessed be He, in the creation of the world; and whoever despises a Torah scholar and those who fear Heaven thereby nullifies the intent of the Holy One, blessed be He. And it is as though he said: His service is not the essential thing! Therefore let people honor the servants of the Holy One, blessed be He, for the honor of the Holy One, blessed be He, to make known that His service alone is the essential thing.
Orchot Tzadikim 24:8: But in honoring the wicked there is desecration of Torah and divine service, and this is a transgression that consumes bone and flesh. And further: many are drawn after them and do as they do, and receive punishment. And of the like of this they said (Mishnah Nega'im 12:6): woe to the wicked man, and woe to his neighbor. And further: honoring the wicked lowers the honor of the righteous, and there is no honor for the righteous except after the lowering of the wicked. And now, since there is a stumbling-block for the world in honoring the wicked, one must be careful not to relate anything good about the wicked. Nor should he mention them favorably, as it is said (Proverbs 10:7), "and the name of the wicked shall rot"; and it is written (ibid. 29:27), "an unjust man is an abomination to the righteous." And if he does not wish to relate the wicked man's wickedness, he should also not relate his good deeds.
Orchot Tzadikim 24:9: The third: a flatterer who praises a wicked man to his face, saying to him, "what a pleasant man and good person you are!" but does not relate his praise publicly, so that it not become a snare for the public. This flatterer's iniquity is also great, as it is written (Proverbs 11:9), "with his mouth the flatterer destroys his neighbor, but through knowledge shall the righteous be delivered." For when he praises him, the wicked man will believe him, and think he is good, and his heart will grow haughty and proud, and he will not repent. For anyone who is not righteous, when praised, will say in his heart: indeed I knew this to be so! And this man is corrupted by this one's flattery.
Orchot Tzadikim 24:10: But the righteous man, if someone praises him, should not become proud because of it, since our Sages, peace upon them, said (Niddah 30b): even if the whole world says you are righteous, be in your own eyes as though wicked. And they said (Avot d'Rabbi Natan 29): if you have friends, some of whom praise you and some of whom discipline and rebuke you, love those who rebuke you and not those who praise you; for these will bring you to eternal life, while those rejoice in your harm when they praise you. And it is said (Proverbs 26:28), "and a flattering mouth works ruin" — he compared a smooth mouth to a slippery path, as it is said (Psalms 35:5-6), "and let the angel of the Lord thrust them away; let their way be dark and slippery," for a person will be thrust away and fall, since a smooth mouth is full of sin and flattery. And of this it is said (ibid. 12:4), "may the Lord cut off all flattering lips, the tongue that speaks proud things." He cursed the smooth mouth for destroying its neighbor, and cursed the harsh tongue, which is the opposite of smoothness, which is slander.
Orchot Tzadikim 24:11: And there are flatterers who flatter men of power so that they will love them, and raise and exalt them; of this our Sages said (Avot d'Rabbi Natan 29:4): whoever flatters his fellow for the sake of honor will in the end depart in disgrace.
Orchot Tzadikim 24:12: The fourth: one who associates with a wicked man — even though he does not flatter him or praise him, but merely draws near to him and associates with him — has a punishment; it is not enough that he does not rebuke him, but he even draws near to him, and he has a punishment for this. And further, punishment is added for the closeness with which he draws near to him, as it is said (2 Chronicles 20:37), "because you have associated with Ahaziah, the Lord has made a breach in your works."
Orchot Tzadikim 24:13: And the righteous despise the wicked. And our Sages of blessed memory said (Bava Kamma 92b): it is not for nothing that the starling goes to the raven, but because it is of its own kind; and so a person who associates with a fellow resembles him. And they said (Megillah 28a): it is forbidden to gaze upon the image and form of a wicked man, as it is said (2 Kings 3:14), "were it not that I regard the presence of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, I would not look at you, nor see you." And whoever gazes upon the form of a wicked man, his eyes will dim in his old age, like Isaac our father, peace upon him, whose eyes dimmed because he gazed upon Esau, even though he did not recognize him for his deeds.
Orchot Tzadikim 24:14: And there is great danger in associating with the wicked: the first, because he thereby loves the enemy of the Maker of all, and no faithful servant of a master associates with his master's enemy. The second, that he learns from his deeds. The third, that others too will associate with him and believe him, and he will rob them, and they too will learn from his deeds; and even if they do not learn from him, they see from him things they are forbidden to see. And also, he himself will not repent, for had they rebuked him and separated from him, he would have turned back from his evil way. And whoever associates with a wicked man is eventually ruled by him; and this is worst of all, for once he rules over him, he will not let him do good. The fourth, that this person must give up doing many good things out of fear [of the wicked man]. Therefore let a person associate only with one who fears Heaven; for whoever Reish Lakish spoke with in the marketplace, people would trust him with merchandise without witnesses (Yoma 9b), for they knew for certain that since he had spoken with him in the marketplace, he was trustworthy. Behold, mere speech is like flattery.
Orchot Tzadikim 24:15: The fifth: a man trusted in the eyes of all the people, whom everyone listens to, who appoints his relative to be a communal leader or a rabbi, and says of him, "I have observed him to be wise" — when this is not so. And so the people rely on him. And likewise he says of one he does not know that he is trustworthy, and the people entrust deposits into his hand — and he lies. And the Sages of blessed memory said (Sanhedrin 7b): whoever appoints an unworthy judge is as though he planted an asherah in Israel; and in a place where there are Torah scholars, it is as though he planted an asherah next to the altar, and the Holy One, blessed be He, is destined to exact payment from the one who appointed him.
Orchot Tzadikim 24:16: The sixth: one who has the power to protest and does not protest, and does not pay attention to the deeds of sinners — this matter is close to flattery. For the sinners think: since they do not protest against us and do not provoke us, all our deeds must be good. And we were commanded to root out evil from among us, as it is said (Deuteronomy 13:6), "and you shall put away the evil from among you."
Orchot Tzadikim 24:17: And our Sages of blessed memory said (Shabbat 54b): whoever has the power to protest against the members of his own household and does not protest is held accountable for the members of his household; against the people of his city, and does not protest, is held accountable for the people of his city; against the whole world, and does not protest, is held accountable for the whole world, as it is said (Leviticus 26:37), "and they shall stumble one upon another"; and our Sages of blessed memory expounded: each because of his brother's iniquity. And we say (Sanhedrin 27b): this teaches that all are sureties for one another.
Orchot Tzadikim 24:18: The seventh: one who sees the people of his place as a stiff-necked people, and says in his heart: perhaps they will not listen if I rebuke them, and therefore refrains from rebuking them. This too is a sin, and he shall bear his iniquity, for he did not try to warn and rebuke them — perhaps they would have repented. And for this completely righteous people were punished at the destruction of the First Temple.
Orchot Tzadikim 24:19: But if the matter is open and known to all, and it has been examined and investigated that the sinner hates discipline and will not listen to those who rebuke him, of this it is said (Proverbs 9:8), "do not rebuke a scoffer, lest he hate you."
Orchot Tzadikim 24:20: And they said: just as it is a commandment to say a thing that will be heeded, so it is a commandment not to say a thing that will not be heeded (Yevamot 65b). And they said: better that they sin unintentionally than deliberately (Shabbat 148b).
Orchot Tzadikim 24:21: The eighth: one who hears words of slander or vulgarity, or sits in the company of scoffers who despise Torah and commandments, and knows that they are stiff-necked and will not accept rebuke, and therefore remains silent. This too is punished, for he should have rebuked them, so that they not say he is like them, agreeing with their words; for he is obligated to reproach them, to give importance to Torah and commandments, and to be zealous for the honor of the righteous man whom they slandered. And he is punished for constantly listening to their bad words when he is unable to answer them each time. And this matter is spelled out in the words of Solomon, peace upon him (Proverbs 24:1-2), "do not envy evil men, nor desire to be with them, for their heart devises violence, and their lips talk of mischief" — meaning: that you will bear their sin, since you constantly hear their words and remain as though silent.
Orchot Tzadikim 24:22: The ninth: one who honors the wicked for the sake of peace. He should not, however, speak well of the wicked man, nor conduct himself with such honor toward him that people think he is important in his eyes deserving of a share of honor; rather, it should be in the manner people honor the rich because their path has prospered, not because of their own worth. And even in this there is sin and guilt, for it is permitted to honor the wicked only out of fear — that one fears the wicked man may harm him and cause him loss at a time when the hand of the wicked is powerful — therefore it is permitted to honor him in the manner people honor men of power. But he should not praise him, nor speak well of him before people. And so our Sages of blessed memory said (Sotah 41b): it is permitted to flatter the wicked in this world. And there are wicked men whom one does not flatter. From where do we know this? From Mordechai, of whom they said, "flatter Haman," and he answered them: "you shall not seek their peace or their good" (Deuteronomy 23:7). And they kept saying to him — our Sages taught: is it not permitted to flatter them for the sake of peaceful relations?! Even so, he did not wish to flatter such a wicked man.
Orchot Tzadikim 24:23: And a person may flatter his wife, for the sake of domestic peace. And likewise his creditor, so he not press him. His teacher, so he teach him Torah. And it is a great commandment to flatter one's students and colleagues, so that they study and heed his words, and accept his rebuke to fulfill the commandments. And likewise, anyone he supposes will be drawn to him, to heed him in fulfilling the commandments, and if approached with anger will not listen, but will accept rebuke only through flattery — it is a great commandment to flatter him, in order to bring out the precious from the vile. For there is a person who accepts rebuke only gently and not with reproach, as it is said (Ecclesiastes 9:17), "the words of the wise, spoken gently, are heeded." And there is one who needs reproach, as it is said (Proverbs 17:10), "a rebuke enters more into a man of understanding." And there is one who needs flogging, as it is said (ibid. 19:29), "and stripes for the back of fools." And there is one for whom even beatings do not help, as it is said (ibid. 17:10), "a hundred blows [do not enter] a fool." If so, what shall we do with him? There is no remedy for him except to drive him away.
Orchot Tzadikim 24:24: And there is a very bad kind of flattery: such as a person who flatters his fellow, and speaks sweet words to him so that he rely on him and trust him. And after his fellow trusts him and relies on him, he deals deceitfully with him. And this is like the matter said (Proverbs 1:17-18), "surely in vain the net is spread in the sight of any bird; and they lay wait for their own blood, they lurk secretly for their own lives." The meaning of the verse: bird-hunters scatter wheat, and birds come to eat the wheat upon the net, and are then trapped — and this flatterer is like that. And the Sages forbade flattery, and said (Chullin 94a) that a person should not send a gift to his fellow knowing he will not eat it. And likewise, if he wishes to open a barrel of wine to sell, and his fellow comes to buy wine, he should not say to him, "I am opening this barrel for your sake." And all this and the like of it is called "stealing the mind." And this the Sages of blessed memory forbade — flattering and stealing people's minds, even the mind of a gentile (ibid.).
Orchot Tzadikim 24:25: Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta said: from the day the fist of flattery grew strong, judgments became perverted and deeds became corrupted, and no person can say to his fellow, "my deeds are greater than yours." Rabbi Elazar said: whoever has flattery in him brings wrath upon the world, as it is said (Job 36:13), "but the flatterers of heart heap up wrath." And not only that, but his prayer is not heard, as it is said (ibid.), "they cry not when He binds them." And even the fetuses in their mothers' wombs curse him, and he falls into Gehinnom. And whoever flatters the wicked falls into his hand; and if he does not fall into his hand, his son falls into his hand; and if his son does not fall into his hand, his grandson falls into his hand (Sotah 41b). Any congregation in which there is flattery is as repugnant as a menstruating woman, as it is said (Job 15:34), "for the congregation of the flatterer shall be desolate." And in the end it is exiled (Sotah 42a).
Orchot Tzadikim 24:26: Therefore let a person keep far from flattery. He should not flatter a person to strengthen him in his wickedness, even if he stands to receive many benefits from him. He should not flatter his relative or his children when they do not walk a good path, for many people persist in their wickedness because they see they feel no shame over their disgraceful ways, and because they see people flattering them. And there is nothing in the world that locks the gates of teshuvah as flattery does.
Orchot Tzadikim 24:27: There is a story of a worthy man who had a daughter to marry off. There were two men beside him, each of whom wished to marry his daughter. This worthy man went and asked one of the men to have a quarrel with him, and in the end brought the two of them to be judged between them, and they did so. One of them flattered this worthy man so that he would marry him his daughter, and declared him right in all his claims. The other said: the law is not with you, but with your fellow. Then the man gave his daughter to the one who had ruled against him, for he said: surely this is a good man, who did not flatter or show me favor (Sefer Chasidim 842).
Orchot Tzadikim 24:28: Therefore whoever is a communal leader, or a judge, or a charity collector, must not be a flatterer. For if the communal leader flatters anyone, and does not rebuke him to do good and turn from evil, then the whole community will be corrupted. For each person will say, "the leader flatters so-and-so," and will not accept his rebuke. And likewise the law of one who flatters one of the litigants — then the words of the other party will be stopped up, and he will not know how to make his claim as he should; it follows that the judgment will not come out truthfully. And likewise flattering charity collectors, who give charity to whoever flatters them, or flatter someone and give to him even though he does not deserve it. Therefore the righteous man must keep very far from flattery, neither flattering nor accepting flattery from others. And he must be very careful, when he performs good deeds, not to intend by them to flatter others, but solely for the sake of Heaven.
Orchot Tzadikim 24:29: And the worst of all flattery: flattering one's fellow in order to cause him to sin. For instance, one who has a dispute with people and the law is not with him, and he flatters people to help him and strengthen his mistaken position. Or one who pursues transgressions such as lewdness and other evils, and flatters his fellow so that he do the same as he does. Therefore Jeroboam ben Nevat merited kingship, because he did not flatter Solomon, but rebuked him regarding the building of the Millo (Sanhedrin 101b).
Orchot Tzadikim 24:30: Whoever wishes to be saved from flattery must be careful to distance himself from honor, for whoever does not concern himself with being honored will not need to flatter. He must also be careful not to benefit from others, for most flatterers flatter people they suppose will be of benefit to them. Therefore whoever distances himself from these two things — benefit and honor — is saved from several transgressions. For many people do good deeds in order to receive honor from people, and this matter corrupts all of a person's service; for many people do good deeds and pray, and have a pleasant voice, and think in their hearts during prayer: "how pleasant is my voice, and people enjoy hearing me." And this is the way of the evil inclination: it does this for every commandment, to catch a person in its net, so that his deeds not be for the sake of Heaven. And likewise regarding benefit: whoever benefits from his fellow, even if he sees him transgressing every transgression in the world, will not be permitted to rebuke him, for he fears he will no longer benefit from him. And this matter is the stumbling-block of the sages of this generation, who pursue benefit from the people — therefore they flatter them so that the people will support them all the more strongly. And it is not enough that they do not rebuke them regarding their affairs, but because they flatter them, they themselves take hold of their deeds and are drawn after them.
Orchot Tzadikim 24:31: It is the nature of a person's creation to be drawn in his mind and his deeds after his companions and friends, conducting himself according to the custom of the people of his region — as they do, so will he do. Therefore a person should associate with the righteous, and always sit among the wise, so as to learn from their deeds; and keep far from the wicked who walk in darkness, so as not to learn from their deeds. And this is what Solomon, peace upon him, said (Proverbs 13:20), "he who walks with the wise shall become wise, but the companion of fools shall be broken." And it says (Psalms 1:1), "happy is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the wicked..."
Orchot Tzadikim 24:32: And likewise, if he is in a region whose customs are bad, and the people of the region do not walk a straight path, let him go to a place whose people are righteous and conduct themselves in good ways. And if all the regions he knows of and hears reports of conduct themselves in a bad way, and he cannot go to a region whose customs are good, because of marauding troops or illness, let him sit alone by himself, as the matter is said (Lamentations 3:28), "let him sit alone and be silent, because He has laid it upon him." And if they are so evil and sinful that they will not let him dwell in the region unless he mingles with them and follows their bad customs, let him go out to caves, thorny places, and deserts, and not conduct himself in the way of sinners, as the matter is said (Jeremiah 9:1), "oh that I had in the wilderness a lodging place for wayfarers" (Rambam, Hilchot De'ot 6:1).
Orchot Tzadikim 25:2: What is slander? Relating the disgrace of one's fellow, even if speaking the truth. But one who speaks falsehood is called "one who gives a bad name." The master of slander is one who sits and says: "so-and-so did such-and-such, his ancestors were such-and-such, I heard such-and-such about him," and says disgraceful things. Of him the verse says (Psalms 12:4), "may the Lord cut off all flattering lips, the tongue that speaks proud things."
Orchot Tzadikim 25:3: And our Sages of blessed memory said: whoever relates slander is as though he denied the fundamental principle [of faith], as it is said (Psalms 12:5), "who have said, with our tongue we will prevail; our lips are our own; who is lord over us?" And therefore slander is a sin, for it does great harm to one's fellow, making his reputation stink in the eyes of the people and causing other losses, while the slanderer himself gains nothing. And certainly whoever is habituated to slander throws off the yoke of Heaven from himself, for he sins without any benefit. And it is worse than a thief or an adulterer, who pursue their own benefit — there is no throwing off of the yoke like slander (Midrash Tehillim 120). And our Sages of blessed memory further said that slander is equivalent to idolatry, forbidden sexual relations, and bloodshed. And this matter is very astonishing, that slander should be equivalent to these transgressions, for each of them one must be killed rather than transgress (Sanhedrin 74a). And they said: idolatry is grave, for whoever denies it is as though he affirmed the entire Torah (Chullin 5a). And they further said (Chullin 4b): one who is an apostate regarding idolatry is an apostate regarding the entire Torah.
Orchot Tzadikim 25:4: And a reason should be given for this matter: the master of the [evil] tongue repeats his folly ten times and more, shaming and disgracing people every day, apart from the harm done to the one he speaks about. And even a light transgression, when a person transgresses it many times, becomes great. For even a single hair, which is soft and very weak, when you gather many hairs together, makes a strong rope from them. And what they said, that slander is equivalent to those three transgressions, means: equivalent to one who transgresses those three transgressions a single time out of the overpowering of his inclination, not equivalent to an apostate who has gone outside the community and transgresses them constantly. And further, the master of slander finds it hard to do teshuvah, since he is habituated to it and has trained his tongue to speak evil. And further, the sin is light in his eyes, for he says, "I have done nothing but mere talk!" and does not take to heart the great harm he causes. And even if he does repent, his teshuvah is not complete, for he does not recognize the greatness of the sin he committed. And he needs forgiveness from those he spoke about, yet he does not remember who they all are. And further, there are cases where he spoke about someone and did him harm, and injured that person, and forgot what he said about him, for slander is hidden and strikes in secret — he is here, yet strikes with his tongue someone far away from him (Arachin 15b) — and this victim is ashamed to make known that he was harmed by him. And sometimes he speaks of a family flaw, harming the generations that come after; and there is no forgiveness for this, for our Sages of blessed memory said (Yerushalmi Bava Kamma 8:7): whoever speaks of a family flaw has no forgiveness, ever.
Orchot Tzadikim 25:5: And further: whoever is habituated to slander sometimes speaks words against the One above, as it is written (Psalms 73:9), "they set their mouth against the heavens, and their tongue walks through the earth." And there is no transgression with a punishment like that of one who utters words against the One above, for our Sages of blessed memory said (Arachin 15a): our fathers were tested with ten trials, and in all of them their sentence was not sealed except for slander, as it is said (Numbers 14:28), "as you have spoken in My ears, so will I do to you"; and it says (Deuteronomy 1:34), "and the Lord heard the voice of your words, and was angry, and swore." And the Torah does not shield masters of slander: Doeg the Edomite — since he related slander, his wisdom did not stand for him, nor did his Torah shield him (Sotah 21a).
Orchot Tzadikim 25:6: And what our Sages of blessed memory said (Sotah, ibid.), that a transgression extinguishes a commandment, but a transgression does not extinguish Torah, as it is said, "for the commandment is a lamp, and the Torah is light" (Proverbs 6:23) — this was said of one who transgresses by way of chance occurrence, not of one who casts off the warning against transgression. Our Sages of blessed memory said (Midrash Tehillim 39): the Congregation of Israel is beloved for her voice, as it is said (Song of Songs 2:14), "let me hear your voice, for your voice is pleasant"; and hated for her voice, as it is said (Jeremiah 12:8), "she has lifted up her voice against Me, therefore I have hated her." Say from this (Proverbs 18:21), "death and life are in the hand of the tongue, and those who love it shall eat its fruit" — the meaning of "one who loves the tongue" is a person who desires to speak always; a proper and sound counsel for him is that he eat its fruit — meaning, that he not speak idle words, but speak only words of Torah and the making of peace, and teach the many to do good, and instruct them in the good and keep them far from evil, and acquire truth. For there is no end to the commandments one can fulfill with the tongue, and this is: "death and life are in the hand of the tongue."
Orchot Tzadikim 25:7: The group of slanderers divides into six parts. The first: one who speaks evil of people because they did the same to him. And sometimes he will cast blame upon a worthy and clean man — then he both lies and slanders. And we were warned in the Torah not to accept slander. And know: when the listener acknowledges the slander, he is as though he were the one relating it, for all those who hear him acknowledge it will say: since he acknowledges it, then the matter must be true. And even if he does not acknowledge it, but merely listens and makes himself appear as though attending to the words and believing them in front of people — through this others too will believe it. And he assists the one relating the slander, for had he rebuked the slanderer, he would have restrained himself from relating more to him. But now, since he listens and shows him a receptive face, he causes him to speak more. And we were warned in a negative commandment (Exodus 23:1), "you shall not accept a false report" — that we not believe a slanderous report in our hearts, holding in our thoughts that the matter is true, and thereby despise in our eyes the person spoken of.
Orchot Tzadikim 25:8: The second: when he speaks slander that is true, if he recalls to himself the bad deeds of that person's ancestors, he transgresses what is written in the Torah (Leviticus 25:14), "you shall not wrong one another" — the verse speaks of wronging through words (Bava Metzia 58b).
